procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but the case originated with the filing of a chargesheet by the NIA.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 19.10.2023 of the High Court of Judicature at Madras in CRLA Nos. 98, 114 and 116 of 2023 and CRLMP Nos. 11595 and 8094 of 2023, which granted bail to the respondents-accused.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The respondents filed Criminal Appeals (CRLA Nos. 98, 114 and 116 of 2023) before the High Court of Judicature at Madras. Some respondents also filed Cr.L.M.P Nos. 11595 and 8094/2023 seeking interim bail. During the pendency of these appeals, the NIA filed a chargesheet against the respondents. The High Court, after considering submissions and materials, allowed the appeals and released the respondents on bail via the order dated 19.10.2023.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Union of India through NIA, Chennai Branch, filed the present set of appeals (Criminal Appeal Nos. 2715-2719 of 2024) in the Supreme Court, being aggrieved by the High Court's order granting bail to the respondents. The appellant argued that the High Court arbitrarily exercised discretion and recorded perverse findings while granting bail. The respondents raised a preliminary objection, arguing that the appeal should be dismissed because the appellant had not disclosed a prior SLP (Crl.) No. 9384/2023 filed against a co-accused for cancellation of bail. The Supreme Court rejected this objection, stating that the prior SLP was not against the same impugned order.

directions: The impugned order passed by the High Court is set aside.
The respondents shall forthwith surrender themselves before the appellant-NIA.
The Special Court shall proceed with the trial as expeditiously as possible and in accordance with law, without being influenced by any of the observations made by this Court in this order.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court improperly and arbitrarily exercised its discretion in granting bail to the accused, warranting interference by the Supreme Court.

facts: The accused-respondents were alleged to be members or office-bearers of the Popular Front of India (PFI), an organization with an alleged anti-national agenda.
The chargesheet contained material, including witness statements and digital evidence, suggesting the accused were involved in recruiting and training members for violent terrorist activities.
The High Court had granted bail to the accused.
The appellant (NIA) challenged the High Court's order, arguing that the discretion to grant bail was exercised improperly and arbitrarily, and that the findings were perverse.
The respondents argued that the evidence was weak and unreliable, and that the High Court had correctly exercised its discretion after considering the material.
law: The standard for challenging an order granting bail is different from an application for cancellation of bail. A challenge to the grant of bail requires showing an improper or arbitrary exercise of discretion by the lower court.

Under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), the proviso to Section 43(D)(5) restricts the grant of bail if there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accusation against the accused is prima facie true.
At the bail stage, a court is not required to conduct a detailed examination of evidence but should form an opinion based on broad probabilities regarding the accused's involvement.
As established in the Watali case, the evidence collected by the investigating agency must be taken at face value at the bail stage and cannot be discarded as unreliable or inadmissible.

While long incarceration can be a ground for bail (as in the K.A. Najeeb case), this principle may not apply if the custody period is not significantly long and other factors like criminal history are present.
application: The Supreme Court determined that its role was to assess whether the High Court had properly applied the law, particularly the restrictive bail conditions under Section 43(D)(5) of the UAPA.

The Court reviewed the chargesheet and other materials and found sufficient evidence (witness statements, digital devices, etc.) to form a prima facie belief that the accusations against the respondents were true.

Applying the principle from the Watali case, the Court rejected the respondents' arguments about the unreliability of witness statements, stating that such an analysis is not permissible at the bail stage.
The Court distinguished the K.A. Najeeb precedent, noting that the respondents had been in custody for only one and a half years (not a long period) and had significant prior criminal histories.

The Court considered the seriousness of the alleged offences, the severity of the prescribed punishment, and the prima facie material collected, concluding that these factors weighed against the grant of bail.

Based on this, the Court found that the High Court had committed a "gross error" by not considering the evidence in its proper perspective and by failing to correctly apply the mandate of Section 43(D)(5) of the UAPA.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had improperly and arbitrarily exercised its discretion in granting bail. It found that there were reasonable grounds to believe the accusations were prima facie true, thus triggering the bail restrictions under the UAPA. Consequently, the Supreme Court accepted the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and directed the respondents to surrender.

issue.issue_text: Whether there was sufficient material in the chargesheet to form a prima facie opinion that the accusations against the respondents under the UAPA were true, thereby attracting the bar on bail under the proviso to Section 43(D)(5) of the UAPA.

facts: The respondents were accused of offences under the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and several sections of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1957 (UAPA).
The High Court had previously granted bail to the respondents.
The Supreme Court was tasked with determining if the chargesheet and other materials presented by the prosecution were sufficient to establish a prima facie case against the respondents.
law: The key legal provision is the proviso to Section 43(D)(5) of the UAPA, which restricts the grant of bail if there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accusation against the accused is prima facie true.
Citing its precedent in the *Watali* case, the Court reiterated that at the bail stage, a detailed examination or dissection of evidence is not required.
The court's role is to form an opinion based on the 'broad probabilities' of the case, taking the material in the chargesheet at face value.
The reliability or admissibility of the prosecution's evidence cannot be questioned at this stage; the material prevails until it is rebutted or disproved at trial.
application: The Supreme Court examined the chargesheet and other materials provided by the investigating agency.
It found that the investigation disclosed PFI's alleged anti-national agenda and that members were motivated towards violent terrorist activities through training.
The evidence included statements from protected witnesses detailing the roles of the respondents, as well as incriminating materials like digital devices, books, and photographs.
The Court noted that this material was sufficient to form an opinion that there were reasonable grounds to believe the accusations were prima facie true.
The Court concluded that the High Court had committed a 'gross error' by not considering this evidence in its proper perspective and deemed its order granting bail 'illegal and perverse'.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the appeal, finding that there was sufficient material in the chargesheet to form a prima facie opinion that the accusations against the respondents were true. Therefore, the bar on bail under the proviso to Section 43(D)(5) of the UAPA was applicable. The Court set aside the High Court's order and directed the respondents to surrender.

issue.issue_text: Whether the commission of a 'terrorist act' as defined under Section 15 of the UAPA is a necessary prerequisite for establishing a prima facie case for an offence under Section 18 of the UAPA.

facts: The High Court had granted bail to the accused, partly on the grounds that the prosecution had not produced material to suggest the commission of any offence falling under Section 15 of the UAPA (the definition of a 'terrorist act').
The prosecution (appellant) had not alleged an offence under Section 15 in the FIR or the chargesheet; the charges were under other sections, including Section 18.
law: Section 18 of the UAPA punishes anyone who conspires, attempts to commit, advocates, abets, advises, incites, or knowingly facilitates the commission of a terrorist act.
Section 18 also criminalizes any act preparatory to the commission of a terrorist act.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court fundamentally misunderstood the scope of Section 18.
The Court clarified that to establish a prima facie case under Section 18, the actual commission of a 'terrorist act' as defined in Section 15 is not required.
Instead, evidence showing that an accused conspired, attempted to commit, or performed any act preparatory to the commission of a terrorist act is sufficient to invoke Section 18.
The Court held that the High Court's insistence on seeing evidence of a completed Section 15 offence to sustain a Section 18 charge was a "patent and manifest error."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the proposition, concluding that the commission of a 'terrorist act' under Section 15 is not a necessary prerequisite for an offence under Section 18. The Court explained that Section 18 is broader and covers preparatory acts, conspiracies, and attempts to commit a terrorist act, even if the act itself is never completed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court improperly and arbitrarily exercised its discretion in granting bail to the accused, warranting interference by the Supreme Court.
appellant_arguments: The appellant implicitly argued that the High Court's discretion was improperly exercised by appealing its decision and contending that the chargesheet material was sufficient to establish a prima facie case, which should have barred bail.
respondent_arguments: The High Court's order was a proper exercise of its discretion after a detailed consideration of the evidence.
The order granting bail was neither illegal nor unjust and should not be interfered with by the Supreme Court.
The appeal should be treated as a 'Second Petition' and not be entertained.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there was sufficient material in the chargesheet to form a prima facie opinion that the accusations against the respondents under the UAPA were true, thereby attracting the bar on bail under the proviso to Section 43(D)(5) of the UAPA.
appellant_arguments: The material recorded in the chargesheet provides reasonable grounds to believe that the accusations against the respondents are prima facie true.
respondent_arguments: The appellant's reliance on statements from protected/listed witnesses was improper because those witnesses had themselves participated in the alleged offences.
The allegations made by the witnesses were vague.
There was no material on record to show any preparatory work done by the respondents to make out a prima facie case against them.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the commission of a 'terrorist act' as defined under Section 15 of the UAPA is a necessary prerequisite for establishing a prima facie case for an offence under Section 18 of the UAPA.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's position, supported by the court's rejection of the issue, is that the commission of a 'terrorist act' under Section 15 is not a prerequisite for an offence of conspiracy or preparation under Section 18.
respondent_arguments: The respondents' position, inferred from the issue and their other arguments about the lack of preparatory work, is that a prima facie case under Section 18 (conspiracy/preparation) requires a connection to a 'terrorist act' as defined in Section 15, which was absent.

cases.case_name: National Investigation Agency v. Zahoor Ahmad Shah Watali
cases.principle: For considering bail under the UAPA, the court must only form an opinion based on the material gathered by the investigating agency as a whole (including the case diary and report under Section 173 CrPC) to determine if there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accusation is prima facie true, without analysing individual pieces of evidence.

cases.case_name: Gurwinder Singh v. State of Punjab and Another
cases.principle: Cited as a recent authority that followed and culled out the guidelines from the Watali case regarding the court's limited role in assessing bail applications under the UAPA.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When determining if an accusation is 'prima facie true', a court must assess if the evidence collected by the investigating agency, on its face, shows the accused's complicity in the offense. This finding is to be based on broad probabilities regarding the accused's involvement, not on proof beyond a reasonable doubt. The evidence must be sufficient to establish the facts of the offense, unless it is rebutted or contradicted.
obiter: The degree of satisfaction required for a court to opine that an accusation is 'prima facie true' is lighter than the standard required under other special enactments to form an opinion that the accused is 'not guilty'.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court found that the High Court committed a gross, illegal, and perverse error in granting bail by failing to properly consider the chargesheet material. The Court held that there was sufficient material—including witness statements, digital devices, and books—to form an opinion based on broad probabilities that there were reasonable grounds for believing the accusations against the respondents were prima facie true. This finding triggered the statutory bar on bail under the proviso to Section 43(D)(5) of the UAPA, making the High Court's order unsustainable and warranting interference.
legal_tests_applied: When challenging an order granting bail on the ground that it was granted illegally, the consideration is whether there was an improper or arbitrary exercise of discretion or if the findings recorded were perverse.

Under the proviso to Section 43(D)(5) of the UAPA, the Court must examine the report under Section 173 Cr.P.C. in its entirety to form an opinion as to whether there are reasonable grounds for believing the accusation against the accused is prima facie true.
At the bail stage, the Court is merely expected to record a finding on the basis of broad probabilities regarding the involvement of the accused, not on proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
For the purpose of considering an offence under Section 18 of the UAPA (conspiracy), the commission of a 'terrorist act' as contemplated in Section 15 of the UAPA is not required to be made out.
policy_considerations: The Court must strike a balance between the civil liberties of the accused, human rights of the victims, and the compelling interest of the state.
National security is always of paramount importance.
